title: How Citizen's Arrests Work
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant explain citizen's arrest: its English common law roots in posse comitatus, the advice that people should generally not attempt one, and how federal and state laws differ. They cover federal search-and-seizure statute language and the 'any person' felony interpretation promoted by the Crime Fighters group, state variations (Kentucky's duty to act, felony-only states, force limits, merchant searches), procedural rules like announcing the arrest and getting police quickly, and the dangers including the Guardian Angels stabbings, the Ricardo Hernandez killing in San Jose, and the Australian death. They also discuss real-life superheroes and activist citizen's arrests. The episode closes with listener mail about Brian Bishop's top five Hollywood remakes list and a first-pitch discussion.
topics: use of force in citizen's arrest

segments.title: Opening banter and the Australian citizen's arrest death
segments.summary: Hosts open with a mock arrest bit and mention a June death in Australia during a citizen's arrest, plus the earlier diamond shop case in London. They say people generally should not perform citizen's arrests, and that calling police or recording video is usually better.

segments.title: Origins in English common law and posse comitatus
segments.summary: The hosts trace citizen's arrest to English common law and the posse comitatus, under which a sheriff could call on able-bodied men to help make arrests. They note that many countries have similar laws and that U.S. cities once relied on citizens because police forces were small, such as Philadelphia with fifteen detectives. H. H. Holmes is cited as caught by a private citizen.

segments.title: Federal law and the Crime Fighters interpretation
segments.summary: The hosts discuss federal law, the Crime Fighters newsletter and its advice, and the wording of Title 18 Section 2236 on searches. They explain the exceptions and how Crime Fighters argues that the word 'person' in the second part lets citizens act on felonies.

segments.title: State laws: felonies, misdemeanors, duty to act, and force
segments.summary: The hosts describe how state laws vary, with some allowing arrests for misdemeanors and others requiring a felony. Kentucky is described as requiring action when a crime is seen, Utah bars deadly force, and some states allow only detention or limited searches. Similar rules are noted in Canada, England, Finland and Norway. Merchant search rights and seizing weapons or drugs in plain view are also covered.
topics: use of force in citizen's arrest

segments.title: Procedure: announcing the arrest, Miranda, and calling police
segments.summary: The hosts explain that citizens generally must announce their intent and get real police on scene quickly, and should not transport suspects in their own car or a taxi. They discuss that Miranda rights do not apply to citizen arrests in the same way, and that a suspect may still talk to a citizen. Crime Fighters' claims about touching suspects are mentioned as dubious.

segments.title: Dangers, lawsuits, and fatal outcomes
segments.summary: The hosts list dangers including the Guardian Angels being stabbed in Chicago in 2012, the 2013 San Jose case in which Ricardo Hernandez killed Christopher Soriano in a fight over a gun, and possible lawsuits for assault, false imprisonment or kidnapping. They conclude it is a bad idea in most situations, except when someone is in real physical danger.

segments.title: Real-life superheroes and activist arrests
segments.summary: The hosts discuss self-styled real-life superheroes such as Phoenix Jones and Dark Guardian, and activist citizen's arrests such as the symbolic arrest of Tony Blair and attempted arrests of oil executives. They also say police warn against such efforts.
topics: Tony Blair arrest for war crimes

segments.title: Wrap-up of citizen's arrest episode
segments.summary: The hosts summarize the advice to avoid citizen's arrests and point listeners to the blog post and further searches.

segments.title: Listener mail: Brian Bishop's top five remakes and first pitch
segments.summary: The hosts respond to Brian Bishop's list of top movie remakes, including Vanilla Sky, The Departed, Ocean's Eleven, The Fly, and 3:10 to Yuma, and discuss a Hollywood remake episode. They also talk about throwing out a first pitch at a professional baseball game.
